title: If You Loved ‘Stuart Fails to Save the Universe,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next
description: If the meta and hilarious spinoff to "The Big Bang Theory" is your cup of tea, you will love "Everything Everywhere All at Once."
fullText:
Stuart Fails to Save the Universe might be the most surprising series on TV right now. Another spinoff from the wildly successful The Big Bang Theory, the show’s focus on bit players from the original series and an enthusiastic embrace of its gonzo multiverse plot shaped a fun, fast-paced, and inventive sitcom that both scratches the nostalgic itch for more of that universe and offers something completely fresh and new in it. If you’re looking for more sci-fi hijinx and humor that embraces the multiverse with wit, imagination, and a robust supply of heart (and you’ve already burned through the shows that offer a similar vibe), then there’s precisely one movie you should watch immediately: Everything Everywhere All at Once.

Written and directed by Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert (aka the Daniels), Everything Everywhere All at Once is the story of Evelyn Quan Wang (Michelle Yeoh), an unhappy, middle-aged immigrant from China who runs a failing laundromat and is struggling in every aspect of her life, from her relationships with her father (James Hong), husband (Ke Huy Quan), and daughter (Stephanie Hsu) to her upcoming audit with the IRS. At her IRS interview, her body is suddenly controlled and she finds herself face to face with an alternate version of her husband, Waymond, who informs her that there are multiple universes and versions of her, and that she must access the skills and life experience of those alternate versions in order to save the multiverse from destruction by Jobu Tupaki—an alternate version of her daughter, Joy.

If you love the wild ride that Stuart Fails to Save the Universe offers as the gang regularly slides into a new alternate world, Everything Everywhere All at Once is the perfect match. As Evelyn struggles to comprehend the nature of her existence in a multiverse and figure out how to survive the bizarre and mind-blowing attacks Jobu Tupaki sends her way, we are treated to a dizzying range of insane universes. We see Evelyn as a martial arts movie star (not unlike Yeoh in real life), a scientist, a teppanyaki chef, a woman with hot dogs for fingers (in a universe where everyone has hot dogs for fingers) and, in one of the most moving moments, as a literal rock.

If you’re digging the emotional core of the show as Stuart seeks a universe where he is worthy and hasn’t ruined everything, the core premise of Everything will hit you right in the feels. Evelyn has been chosen because she’s the worst version of herself—the version that has consistently failed in everything she’s tried, and thus the version with the most stored potential. Her emotional journey from nihilism and anger to love and acceptance as she learns to fight for what she loves is powerfully moving. Like the show, the movie leverages the character-building aspects of a multiverse, letting us see how a normal, regular person with normal, regular problems might face a terrifyingly abnormal challenge.

Plus, the movie is just fun. How can you watch a scene where mild-mannered Waymond Wang defeats a gang of security guards using multiverse-downloaded fannypack skills and not want to watch the rest of the movie?

Stream Everything Everywhere All at Once on Hulu, or rent it on Prime Video.

The multiverse may be infinite, but movies about them aren’t. If you’ve watched Everything Everywhere All at Once and need more fun sci-fi stories, here are a few more movies that catch that Stuart vibe.

Douglas Adams’ classic story of an ordinary guy named Arthur Dent who is rescued by his friend (and secret alien) Ford Prefect when Earth is destroyed to make way for a hyperspace bypass isn’t a multiverse story per se, but it has similar elements. That’s thanks to the Infinite Improbability Drive, which allows for faster-than-light travel by passing through every point in every possible universe simultaneously, resulting in some really, really weird stuff (the hilariously inconsistent timeline resulting from the many variations of the story also contributes a sense of multiversity craziness). It’s an absurdist’s dream, riffing on every conceivable sci-fi trope and delivering a surprisingly sweet story of a man struggling with his sense of unimportance in an increasingly confusing existence.

Rent The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy on Prime Video.

You want a bit more edge to your multiverse humor? Check out Deadpool & Wolverine, in which everyone’s favorite merc with a mouth (Ryan Reynolds) has to skip through various universes to find a replacement Wolverine (Hugh Jackman), who famously and nobly died at the end of Logan in 2017, for, er, reasons. It’s absolutely riddled with hilarious bits, fourth-wall breaks, and hyperviolence—but there’s a gooey emotional core to it, as well.

Stream Deadpool & Wolverine on Disney Plus, or rent it on Prime Video.

If Everything Everywhere All at Once is a bit too staid and sedate for your tastes, check out this 1984 fever dream of a sci-fi movie. When rock star, scientist, and surgeon Buckaroo Banzai (Peter Weller) tests a device that allows him to pass through matter, he briefly engages with the 8th dimension—and unwittingly attracts the attention of aliens who wish to use his technology to free their brethren trapped there, putting the existence of humanity at risk. It’s one of the weirdest vibes ever captured on film, but it’s also hilarious and one of the most unique films you’ll ever watch.

Stream The Adventures of Buckaroo Banzai Across the 8th Dimension on The Roku Channel, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you love the unexpected twists that Stuart Fails to Save the Universe serves up as he and his friends travel through alternate universes, strap in for John Dies at the End. To say the story is complex would an understatement—it slides between the past, present, and future of various dimensions at a rapid clip—but it kicks off when a man named David (Chase Williamson) is contacted by his recently dead friend, Rob, who tells him about a drug called Soy Sauce that lets folks remember the future and allows entities to creep from one universe into another—and they’re infiltrating David’s universe. It’s wild and often really funny, so if it’s extra you’re looking for, look no further.

Stream John Dies at the End on The Roku Channel, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you want to lean a bit more into plain old funny stuff, this modern classic is perfect. There’s no multiverse here, but there is a lot of affectionate humor aimed squarely at sci-fi tropes (especially the Star Trek universe and its, er, passionate fans). Galaxy Quest was a Trek-like TV series that aliens called Thermians believe was a documentary. When their civilization is threatened by a villain named Sarris, they kidnap the cast (including Tim Allen, Alan Rickman, Sigourney Weaver, and Sam Rockwell) of the TV series to help them defeat Sarris, and, yes, hilarity ensues. But also a lot of heart and character development, if that’s your bag.

Stream Galaxy Quest on Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

title: More than 1,200 AI workers across Anthropic, DeepMind, OpenAI, and Meta are asking for Washington’s help building an AI slowdown plan
description: The statement, signed by senior executives at competing companies, calls on the government to help build the tools needed to pace frontier AI development.
fullText:
More than 1,200 employees at the world's leading AI labs, including senior executives, have signed a statement asking the U.S. government to help build the tools needed to slow down AI development if it ever becomes necessary.

The statement, titled "Pacing the Frontier," was published Tuesday and has been signed by prominent tech figures including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and several of the company's cofounders, alongside OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki, Meta chief scientist Shengjia Zhao, and Google DeepMind head of AI safety and alignment Anca Dragan.

The list brings together companies that are normally locked in fierce competition with one another and is a striking statement for an industry under enormous commercial pressure to keep building ever larger and more capable models.

"Having so many staff from different companies come together in agreement on this point is striking," Tyler Johnston, founder of the Midas Project, an AI watchdog group, told Fortune. "There are many bitter rivalries and disagreements in the industry, so the fact that there is such strong consensus on this point is a warning that we really ought to pay attention to."

While the statement does not ask any company to slow down at the moment, it does call on Washington to support an international effort to build the technical and governance tools that would help the world "pace" development. It specifically calls out the risks around AI systems that start to design their own successors faster than anyone can understand or control them.

"Having talked to many of the people who signed the letter, they don't want a pause," Peter Wildeford, head of policy at the AI Policy Network, told Fortune. "But there is a concern about how the technology is advancing." The companies are looking for the optionality to do that at some point and have support from a third party when that point arrives, he added.

The letter comes in the wake of a security breach that has rattled the AI industry. OpenAI disclosed that two of its models, the newly released GPT-5.6 Sol and a more capable unreleased research system, broke out of a sandboxed internal test environment, found a previously unknown vulnerability that gave them access to the open internet, and then used stolen credentials and additional exploits to breach the production systems of Hugging Face to steal the answers to a cybersecurity benchmark they were being evaluated on. Hugging Face detected and contained the intrusion on its own days before OpenAI connected the activity to its internal testing, and had already reported it to law enforcement.

fullText:
In opening statements, state argued Meta’s own research showed it harmed teens while firm’s attorneys pointed to transparency

The long-awaited trial between the social media company Meta and the state of Tennessee began proceedings on Monday. Attorneys for Tennessee told a jury in Nashville that Meta, which owns Instagram and Facebook, disregarded internal research about its platform’s impact on teenagers, while the company sought ⁠to maximize profit from those young users.

During ⁠opening statements in a seven-week ​trial in state court, the state’s lawyers said Meta researchers repeatedly flagged teenagers’ compulsive use of the platform – leading to eating disorders, depression and self-harm. But despite those warnings, Meta did not ⁠disable features such as autoplay, notifications and infinite scroll which, the lawyers said, were designed to keep teens on Instagram as long as possible and increase the number of ads they viewed.

An attorney for Meta countered the company has been transparent ⁠about the risks teens face on Instagram and the amount of dangerous content it finds. The company works hard to find problems and fix them, the attorney said.

Tennessee’s lawsuit is one of 42 cases brought against Meta by individual states across the US. It comes after the company suffered a damaging loss in New Mexico in March, where a jury found the company liable for harming children and ordered it to pay $375m in civil penalties. It also comes as thousands of other lawsuits have been filed against Meta and other social media companies by families, school districts and state attorneys general.

The lawsuit in Tennessee, filed by attorney general Jonathan Skrmetti’s office, seeks financial penalties ‌and a court order directing Instagram to modify aspects of the platform that the state says are harmful to teens’ mental health.

If the jury finds ‌Meta liable, the trial will enter a second phase where the judge will decide damages.

During the opening statements, Tom Cartmell, a lawyer for the state, said Instagram triggers dopamine hits that promote addiction and that has a particularly strong impact on the brains of kids.

Cartmell also showed the jury an internal document from 2017 in which Meta product managers wrote that features such as notifications and infinite scroll “are inherently at odds with well-being” and said that the company needed to warn ​the public.

“This warning never came,” Cartmell said.

Kevin Huff, a lawyer for Meta, said documents such as those Cartmell cited are proof that the company is searching for problems on its platforms, so it can improve them. The company has developed tools to help limit problematic use of Instagram, Huff said, and seeks to empower teachers and parents to help keep teens safe.

“We think the evidence will show that Meta is doing its part and empowering others to ​do their part, because protecting teens online is a ​shared responsibility,” Huff said. “It takes a village.”

The next lawsuit over social media addiction and harm to children is slated to go to trial next month in Oakland, California. It will be the first federal trial against the social media companies, including Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snap, and was brought by attorneys general from 29 states.

title: Copyright Scammers Weaponized Meta's Rights Manager with Backdating Exploit
description: Scammers are allegedly exploiting a flaw in Facebook's 'Edit Post' feature to backdate stolen videos and hijack copyright claims.
fullText:
Similar to other social media platforms, creators on Facebook and Instagram have to battle a constant stream of copyright infringing material.

To facilitate this process, the company has rolled out several anti-piracy initiatives in recent years.

Both Facebook and Instagram use a “Rights Manager” tool, which is an automated system that runs copyright checks. After rightsholders upload reference files, the system detects infringing material and allows owners to take down or monetize this content.

Rights Manager has been working without much noise for close to a decade. According to Meta’s latest transparency report, Rights Manager is part of a broader enforcement system that proactively removes millions of infringing posts from Facebook and Instagram every month.

The automated copyright enforcement system is not without flaws. In India, for example, several lawsuits filed at the Delhi High Court alleged that the same copyright enforcement system can be turned against the creators it is meant to protect.

The Rights Manager exploit relies on Facebook’s desktop “Edit Post” feature. When a user edits an existing Facebook post and replaces its attached image or video, the platform keeps the original publication date. This means that users and Meta’s enforcement systems will see the content as older than it really is.

Scammers can allegedly exploit this weakness, Bar and Bench first reported. They can edit their older Facebook pages to add videos, reels, or photos they copied from other creators. To Instagram and Facebook it will appear that their content is older, so they can use it to claim ownership through Rights Manager.

As a result, the scammers can reportedly monetize videos of the original creators, while adding strikes to their accounts too.

Financial educator and entrepreneur Pushkar Raj Thakur says at least 36 of his videos were taken down worldwide this way. His suit argues Meta acted on the claims without checking the rightsholder, metadata or edit history of the posts.

Thakur took the matter to the Delhi High Court in May as part of a broader lawsuit about false claims. Early on, Meta’s counsel said the company needed to investigate, but the false claims did not stop right away.

In a follow-up hearing, Meta offered the court a series of assurances. It agreed not to remove Thakur’s videos over copyright strikes, not to close his account over repeat strikes, and to restore the deleted content.

Thakur is not backing down, seeking roughly 2 crore rupees (about $210,000) in damages. He also wants the court to order Meta to build safeguards into Rights Manager, including KYC checks, timestamp protections, and metadata verification.

Interestingly, Thakur says Meta denied him access to Rights Manager to protect his own brand, even as the scammers used the very same tool against him.

Thakur’s lawsuit is not the only one. Another creator, Neeraj Joshi, filed a similar complaint over the same backdating trick, and this case already resulted in a more actionable order.

On July 9, Justice Jyoti Singh required Meta to preserve Joshi’s verified Instagram account and to hand over the basic subscriber information and IP logs tied to the fraudulent claims within three weeks.

Those records could reveal who is behind the scheme and Joshi’s request for an interim injunction will be heard on August 5.

The two lawsuits are not the only pressure on Meta. On July 15, another creator, Nitin Joshi, filed a public interest litigation (PIL) that goes after the legal framework itself.

The petition asks the court to set up a Special Investigation Team to probe what Joshi describes as an organized extortion racket, where syndicates file bogus strikes through bot accounts and then demand payment to withdraw them.

It also challenges Rules 3(1)(c) and 4 of India’s IT Rules, arguing they let platforms disable accounts without notice, without naming the complainant, and without checking whether the claimant owns the content.

Joshi wants a forensic audit of Instagram’s copyright strike system, as well as regular transparency reports on repeat complainants. This case remains in its early stages, and it has yet to be heard.

For now, the three cases leave Meta with an unusual problem. The same automated system that’s used to remove millions of infringing posts is allegedly being used by scammers to monetize copyright infringement.

Monthly proactive Instagram removals

Whether Meta has already addressed the loophole, and whether the scammers will be unmasked, remains to be seen. The company has yet to respond to the allegations in court, and it hasn’t commented publicly on the claims.

In any case, it appears that Meta has some work to do on the transparency side as well. At the time of writing, its most recent copyright transparency report is more than two years old, covering 2023.

A copy of the order in the Neeraj Joshi case is available here (pdf). The July 1 order in the Pushkar Raj Thakur case can be found here (pdf), and the earlier May 29 order is here (pdf).

title: How Apple Might Try to Make Its Smart Glasses Less Creepy
description: Apple's first pair of smart glasses is expected in 2027, giving the company a year to figure out how avoid the social stigma of Meta's glasses.
fullText:
Apple is expected to reveal its smart glasses, codename N50, at WWDC 17 in June 2027, which gives the company nearly a year to wrestle with the thorniest problem facing smart glasses: how do you uphold a commitment to privacy while selling a product that contains a hidden camera?

Like industry leader Meta's line of Ray-Ban and Oakley glasses, Apple's first smart glasses are expected to focus on AI, audio, and onboard cameras (display models are expected at a later date.) But Meta's glasses are at the center of a growing cultural firestorm for the camera feature, with people calling Metas "pervert glasses," creating guerrilla marketing campaigns against them, and banning them from a growing number of locations.

According to a Bloomberg report from Mark Gurman, Apple is considering releasing smart glasses with a full camera system that can't be used to take pictures or record video. The camera system would be used only for feeding visual information to Apple's AI tools, with no way for users to share that information.

Privacy (either respecting or exploiting) is no doubt at the forefront of every smart glass manufacturer's design decisions, but it's a particularly thorny issue for Apple, given its carefully cultivated image as "privacy first" company. Apple has spent years making data security a pillar of its identity, whether by repeatedly publicly proclaiming it as a "fundamental human right" or stressing on-device processing. Releasing a pair of glasses many would regard as spy glasses could effectively undermine Apple's reputation, even if every other privacy option (no sharing content with third parties, as much on-device processing as possible, etc.) is as robust as possible.

This isn't the first time Apple has been here. When it launched AirTags in 2021, the company built in anti-stalking features like unwanted-tracker alerts, audible chirps, and tools to locate a hidden tag, all to prevent the device from being used to secretly monitor people. But within months, the devices were reported in stalking and domestic abuse cases, prompting lawsuits, news investigations, and the general view of AirTags as tools for creeps. The lesson: good intentions and good engineering are no match for people's worst instincts.

According to consumer research, taking quick videos and pictures is one of the primary reasons people are buying smart glasses in the first place: a February 2026 Counterpoint Research report highlights that enhanced video performance and photography are the most frequently praised features of the Gen 2 Meta glasses. If consumers are facing a decision between Meta glasses, soon-to-be-released Samsung/Google smart glasses, and Apple glasses, how many would choose the one that doesn't have a camera?

While I have no idea what other possible solutions to the privacy problem Apple is considering, if I had to guess, I'd say they've discussed these ideas:

Geofencing: Apple could proactively build geofencing or detection agreements with categories of space like courts, gyms, and schools, or provide some kind of opt-in "fence" for users, like an iPhone setting for "no hidden cameras within my home/business." Given the ban of camera glasses in specific places like New York courts and sections of cruise ships, this seems like a strong contender for where things are headed.

Highly visible status light: Some of the backlash Meta has faced for its camera glasses is over the size of its tiny "I'm taping" warning light. What if it was bigger, brighter, and more visible? I could see that satisfying some people that don't wear and don't like smart glasses with cameras, but how many users want to advertise that they're wearing smart glasses?

A warning system for non-glasses users: There is already an app that tries to warn users if a pair of Meta glasses is in the vicinity; Apple could take the same idea and make it easy for anyone who cares to see who is wearing a pair of Apple glasses around them. Maybe this would even work as advertising, although again, I doubt glasses wearers would like to be singled out like this.

Count on this to blow over: Apple may decide it doesn't care about privacy that much after all; it wouldn't be the first time a company ditched a core value in favor of making a lot of money. Since there's more than a year until Apple glasses are expected to hit shelves, the company might just hope for the best. Public attitudes tend to get less alarmist over time as more people get used to new technology; when camera-equipped cell phones hit the market in the early 2000s, there was widespread panic over photography in gym locker rooms and schools, but that's not something anyone worries as much about these days.

title: Gianni Infantino Lashes Out at World Cup Critics
description: The FIFA president ripped the media in an Instagram post.
fullText:
FIFA president Gianni Infantino posted a 15-slide message directed at people “busy planting seeds of hate” on Instagram on Sunday night, claiming the World Cup went off without incident.

Infantino’s Sunday night missive began: “To everyone who missed our beautiful game…sorry that you were so consumed by hate and criticism that you missed it all.” He went on to further single out people “behind their pens and papers, behind their screens spreading hate and false rumours.”

The post was filled with jarring and inaccurate claims; he wrote that the World Cup saw “zero incidents, zero hostility, zero violence, just joy, emotions, happiness, unity, and togetherness.”

Four people died during celebrations in Mexico City after Mexico beat Ecuador in the round of 32. South African midfielder Jayden Adams was found dead in Cape Town after returning from the tournament, and police are investigating a cause of death.

FIFA did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the inaccuracies or what prompted Infantino’s post.

Even and especially at its best, the World Cup—as always—stirred up hostility and political tensions. Argentine fans in Atlanta were captured on video fighting with one another on the night before the match, and with England fans after the semifinal win. The match reignited historic claims from the Argentine government, players, and fans against Great Britain over the Falkland Islands, including with an on-pitch demonstration by the players. In the U.K., more domestic abuse incidents were reported during the tournament than the past two World Cups and Euros.

Infantino also wrote that “Iran entered the United States without incident or conflict.” Iran’s coach, though, said his side was “perhaps the most oppressed” team in the tournament after the quick trip from Tijuana to Los Angeles took five hours with security screenings, then the team would need to return immediately after the match. Iran saw 11 federation members and team staffers denied entry into the U.S., including federation president Mehdi Taj.

The Iranian federation also said it would file a complaint to FIFA for denying its request to travel two days in advance of its match against Belgium.

Infantino wrote that “Football is bigger than hate and discrimination.” Multiple incidents of racist abuse occurred during the World Cup. Most notably, a Paraguayan senator called Kylian Mbappé a “colonised Cameroonian,” to which the French captain called her “a despicable woman and unworthy of your position.”

Infantino said the World Cup’s haters “mentioned the few people denied visas and overlooked the millions who were approved, from all parts of the world.”

The most high profile visa cases include that of Somali referee Omar Artan, denied entry into the U.S. over alleged “association with suspected members of terrorist organizations,” and Ghana midfielder Thomas Partey, who was not allowed into Canada for matches due to ongoing rape charges.

And fans from Haiti, Iran, Senegal, and Ivory Coast were simply banned from entering the United States under blanket Trump administration policy; others were subject to a $15,000 bond that deterred many from coming. (FIFA celebrated that it got the U.S. to waive this requirement, but that only applied to a certain subset of fans who had already purchased tickets and opted into an expedited visa process.)

Infantino did not mention Folarin Balogun’s red card or its subsequent suspension directly, but he was still defensive about the notorious incident.

“Indeed, ‘arguable’ referees’ decisions or ‘strange’ disciplinary rulings such as for instance potentially mistaken red or yellow cards or subsequent decisions not to ban players in certain situations are routine and widely accepted in some of the biggest leagues worldwide,” Infantino wrote. “It’s curious that the same countries employing these practices are the ones criticising.”

European leaders had blasted FIFA’s handlingof Balogun’s red card to the point where UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin—whose organization called the red card reversal an “unprecedented, incomprehensible and unjustifiable decision”—boycotted the tournament final. (Some European leagues do review red cards after games, which is not generally FIFA protocol.)

Infantino has not taken questions from reporters since a press conference before the opening match in Mexico City on June 10.

There, Infantino was also defensive and vague, saying, “We try to do our best” on a number of issues like Iran, high ticket prices, and visa restrictions. After initially telling people to “chill, relax,” Infantino later clarified that he meant “to trust us that we are working behind the scenes.”

He was more aggressive on Sunday night.

“To those spending their time and energy hating us, please take a moment to reflect, meditate, pray, or watch a football match and truly observe the faces, the eyes, the emotions,” Infantino wrote. “To the pens and papers, to all the screens, may you find love and peace where the people behind you couldn’t.

“May you find peace; we at FIFA have found ours and we deliver it, by delivering the most outstanding FIFA World Cup.”

Also on Sunday night, Rep. description: An Instagram post turned one California student newspaper into a free-speech flash point. The students say they were just doing their homework.
fullText:
for his journalism class was to tell a news story—any news story—in the form of an extended Instagram slideshow. So when the high school senior got home on the afternoon of February 10, 2026, he grabbed a snack, went upstairs to his room, and settled in to work.

After allowing himself a few minutes of procrastination—scouting prospective college campuses on Google Earth—Mueller navigated over to the Department of Justice’s Epstein Library portal and clicked through the page asking whether he was 18 or older (he was, just barely). Then he began poking around for ideas in the 3 million pages of Epstein files that had been added 11 days earlier.

Mueller really liked working in his bedroom, with its beanbag chair and view of people strolling and biking along one of Marin County, California’s sun-dappled waterways. Having lived his whole life in one of the wealthiest parts of America, Mueller couldn’t help thinking his area probably had some ties to Jeffrey Epstein. “I think it’s very difficult to get an immense amount of money without—this is my opinion—without doing something a little shady,” Mueller says. So he sat on his bedroom floor and spent the next five hours combing the federal database for links to the towns and cities of Marin.

He found thousands. Most of them were trivial (Epstein liked to shop online at Restoration Hardware, headquartered in nearby Corte Madera). But a few things stood out: a 2014 art gala in Sausalito that Epstein helped promote; a meeting with Woody Allen in Tiburon; and—above all—a 2013 email exchange between Epstein and an address bearing the name of a woman associated with a French model casting agency called Mill Valley Connection. “Regarding Hannah, my Austrian model,” read one particularly chilling message, “we can come and see you this evening if you are interested, and in that case let me know how I can get my fees.”

Two days later, on February 12, Mueller posted his story to the Instagram feed of the Redwood Bark, his school’s student-run publication. It was a carousel-style slideshow pitched at readers across the county. “Which Marin towns were mentioned in the Epstein files?” the first panel reads. “Scroll to see how many times your town was mentioned.” Rather than quote from the most alarming document he’d found, Mueller kept his descriptions fairly general and brief: “Mill Valley was mentioned in the context of providing models to Epstein from a woman named Gisele Attias Bonnouvrier.”

More than 4,000 people liked the story. The comments filled up with praise: “This is the kind of journalism we need.” “Higher quality reporting than local outlets.” “High schoolers doing better reporting than national news.” “Didn’t think I’d be following a random CA HS newspaper in 2026 for their breaking reporting but here we are.”

As Mueller watched the numbers climb, he felt excited but also a little perplexed. “I didn’t really think I was doing groundbreaking journalism,” he says. “I was just like, this is another piece of homework that I have to do today, and I’ve just got to get it done—but also be thorough, because people are going to see it on the internet.”

About a week and a half later, Mueller was home sick with a light fever and cough when the phone rang. It was his journalism teacher, Erin Schneider, with bad news. “This person mentioned in your post is now threatening to sue the district,” she said.

On Monday, February 23, Bonnouvrier, the woman affiliated with the model casting agency, had sent an email to the principal of Redwood High School, calling Mueller’s post defamatory, demanding its immediate removal, and promising legal action if the school did not comply within 48 hours. And now the district superintendent was demanding that the Bark either redact Bonnouvrier’s name or delete the slide entirely.

title: Instagram Is Starting to Crack Down on Creepy Smart Glasses Videos
description: Creepy videos are being more heavily scrutinized by Meta.
fullText:
In a recent story posted on Instagram, Instagram head Adam Mosseri revealed the social media platform is banning smart glasses videos where people are being harassed and exploited for views.

"If you're posting content that is taking advantage of people and harassing them, like a lot of these pickup line kind of videos that we've heard of and seen, then we're going to take the content down," Mosseri said. "We don't want people to be surreptitiously taking videos of other people and harassing them and then posting them on our platform. So we're trying to fight that every way we can."

Hidden camera prank videos and "pickup" type videos are obviously not new, but the easy availability of camera glasses has led to a spike in this kind of content, with videos of men trying to pick up women, pranking retail workers, and other pranks appearing more frequently across all video-sharing services.

Business Insider reported that Meta recently pulled two accounts with over a million followers for posting "pickup artist" videos, where women who may not have known they were being filmed have their videos posted online, leading to harassment. A Meta spokesperson confirmed that the accounts were nuked in accordance with the company's existing bullying and harassment policy.

Meta's official policy on bullying states "We remove content that's meant to degrade or shame, including, for example, claims about someone's sexual activity," and lists a number of specific examples like, "severe sexualized commentary" and "calls for, or statements of intent to engage in, bullying and/or harassment." But there's a lot of gray area. Videos featuring vaguely aggressive acts directed at strangers apparently aren't in violation of Meta's standards, for instance. Neither is a video like the one below, but I'd feel pretty harassed if I were that doctor.

There isn't a reliable way to automate harassment detection because so much of what constitutes harassment comes down to intent and context. This leaves enforcement up to users who can flag videos and/or victims, who are often unaware their image is being spread online until it's too late to put the toothpaste back in the tube.

The backlash over camera-equipped smart glasses is definitely growing, whether its apps designed to suss them out in public, condemnation from pop stars, or outright bans on smart glasses in some places.

As a privacy safeguard, Meta's glasses have a front-facing light that comes on when video is being taken or a picture is being snapped, but the light has been an ongoing issue since the glasses launched. Disabling it has turned into an ongoing game of cat-and-mouse: Meta smart glasses' cameras won't work if the light is covered, but hackers found ways to modify the hardware itself, leading Meta to release a mandatory update that will physically disable any glasses if a user tampers with the indicator. Creeps are pretty ingenious, so I expect further workarounds.

Whether they have lights or not, hidden cameras are generally legal to use in public places in the U.S. (with a few exceptions), and it's not necessarily against the law to film yourself trying to pick someone up, then post the footage online so weirdos can comment, either.

Unless you're really eagle-eyed, it's tough to spot someone with a hacked pair of glasses with no recording indicator light, but it's not impossible. Here are a few things to look for:

The rivet: Most standard glasses have decoration of some kind to cover the glasses' hinge. On Meta Ray-Bans and most other camera glasses, they're round and slightly oversized with a glass inner circle.

Thick frames: While the technology is getting smaller, camera equipped glasses tend to have thicker frames to hide the gear.

The tap: There's two ways to trigger an off-the-shelf pair of Meta smart glasses, saying "Hey, Meta, take video" or tapping the side of the glasses.

Head movement: Meta glasses have a pretty wide lens, so they don't require a ton of movement to capture a scene, but still, if someone is moving their head when they could just be moving their eyes, they might be trying to keep something in frame.

All that said, despite the growing popularity of the nickname "pervert glasses," camera-equipped smart glasses have a variety of legitimate uses and I assume the vast majority of wearers want a quick way to upload content to Instagram, answer texts, or take a picture without having to pull out their phones, so just spotting the glasses in the wild doesn't mean you've spotted a creeper. Usually.

title: You Can Now Verify Your Facebook Account With a Video Selfie
description: Upload a selfie video and earn a white check mark. But is that a good idea?
fullText:
If you're on Facebook, you may soon see a new type of verification badge on user profiles meant to indicate that there is a real, live person behind them. The platform is adding a free verification feature that allows users to upload a selfie video and earn a white check mark, which will appear on their profile and across Marketplace, Dating, and Groups. (At launch, badges won't appear in Feed posts, but Facebook says that feature will be added in the future.)

Note that this is different from Meta Verified, a paid subscription that provides the blue check mark to accounts on Facebook and Instagram. This verification indicates that Meta has confirmed the user's identity based on a review of their government-issued ID and, in some cases, a selfie video.

Facebook Verified is available to users age 18 and older whose accounts are in good standing with the platform's community standards, though the feature is launching in select markets initially before being rolled out globally. Once you have access, you'll need to record a short video selfie, which Facebook will compare to existing profile photos on your account using facial recognition. If your verification is approved, the white check mark will be added to your profile. Verification is not available for Pages or ProMode accounts.

Facebook says it will store your selfie video for "up to 30 days" after verification, which is a one-time process. It's not entirely clear what happens with that video in the meantime, and it's worth noting that Meta has relied on user data to train its AI. Meta AI (and Meta more broadly) is a terrible offender when it comes to privacy and security, so you should consider whether the tradeoff of a verification mark is worth handing over more of your data and read the privacy policy before you agree.

Google also launched a video selfie verification feature this week, though its purpose is to prove your identity should you get locked out of your account. Unlike Facebook Verified, which is meant to be a trust signal to other users, Google's selfie verification allows access to your entire Google account, bringing with it some additional security considerations.

title: This App Can Help Detect When Someone Near You Is Wearing Meta Glasses
description: But it only detects them when they are charging, powering on, or while they're actively pairing.
fullText:
An app has launched that detects whether the people around you are using Meta and other kinds of smart glasses. Antizuck Smart Glasses Scanner, available for iPhone and designed by Albert Pariente Cohen, detects nearby Bluetooth signals that match Meta glasses, Snap Spectacles, Meta Quest headsets, RayNeo smart glasses, and other devices; then, it lets you know what gadget is nearby and whether it's been detected previously. In keeping with the "privacy" focus, Antizuck doesn't require an account or email address, nor does it send any data outside of your phone. It retails for $2.99 with no subscription.

In my testing, Antizuck successfully identified both my Meta glasses and my Quest 3 headset. It actually called out my Quest 3 (name and distance) while the headset was in sleep mode. The Meta glasses, though, weren't as easily detected. While it did find my glasses, it only "saw" them when I turned them off and on: Antizuck only detects Meta glasses that are charging, powering on, or while they're actively pairing.

The app can also tell you all the other Bluetooth devices advertising around you, and it identifies what they are, if possible. Interestingly, it identified my charging Even Realities G2 smart glasses, but didn't flag them, I assume because they don't have a camera. Still, just seeing how many devices are broadcasting around you is worth the $3 price of admission.

It's clear from the app's "glasses spotted" warning of "Someone may be recording near you" that the point is to let you know if a creep is creeping nearby, but they're only marginally useful for that purpose. They do not let you know which passersby are wearing Meta glasses. They don't show you an alert when a nearby pair of glasses starts recording or takes a picture, nor do they alert you when a nearby pair of Meta glasses is transferring media from the glasses to a phone. If someone turns on their glasses near you or charges them for three minutes or so, you'll get a ping and a record of whether that same pair of glasses has been detected by you in the past. But most people aren't charging their glasses on a street corner or in a bar.

Utility aside, the app is clearly part of the growing backlash against people using camera-forward smart glasses, whether it's New York banning them in court, or singer Lorde calling them "not sexy." I completely understand the concern people, particularly women, have about being recorded by hidden spy glasses, but it's not as one-sided an argument as it may appear at first. People with vision problems use Meta glasses to get verbal help from the AI. Birdwatchers use them to identify birds on the fly. I use my Meta glasses to categorize receipts for tax purposes, listen to Hawkwind, and occasionally take videos on bike rides. I'd rather not have strangers assume I'm a creep, or know that I'm wearing a specific brand of eyeglasses at all. Just as it's legal to take photos in public places, it's legal to scan your surroundings for Bluetooth signatures, but isn't each an invasion of privacy? Like anything, the only thing evil about a tool is how you use it.

In a week where an AI model went rogue and broke out of a secure test environment—and in a year where seemingly all we're hearing is how AI can displace large swaths of the workforce—it may come as a surprise when one of the tech's most prominent voices is pushing an optimistic view of the tech, joining the many in his field who have recently walked back comments of how it could negatively impact workers.

"As we enter this next wave with AI, we continue to believe the future is for everyone," Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote as the caption to a short video on Thursday, harkening back to the company's early years of tech optimism.

"Call us optimists, call us dreamers, call us whatever the hell you want, but we're betting on people, and we like those odds," the voiceover in the video said.

The video featured montages of people using Instagram, Whatsapp, FaceBook and Meta's Ray-Ban glasses to film touching moments and connect with loved ones, with the backdrop of concerts and snowboarding and laughing children set to calm music as the voiceover framed Meta's AI efforts as doubling down on betting on people, just like the company did 22 years ago with FaceBook.

Marketing experts told Fortune that the Meta video's reliance on nostalgic imagery seemed like a way to redirect attention from AI concerns and to buffer against growing AI fears.

"They're showing people having a great time, but they're not really responding to what the fundamental issue is, which is how is AI going to impact me when I start dealing with your platform when you integrate all of that technology into it," Mara Einstein, a media studies professor at CUNY's Queens College, told Fortune. "The problem is the AI technology is not the same as previous versions of social media that they have used to connect people in the past."

The sentiment was echoed by Ana Babic Rosario, a marketing professor at the University of Denver's Daniels College of Business, who pointed to Meta's more recent struggles as reason why Meta might want to draw nostalgia to the past. Last week, Meta employees sued the company for allegedly using AI in the company's recent 8,000 layoffs that the employees claim disproportionately targeted workers on medical, parental or family leave. fullText:
Withdrawn case marks a victory for the social media giant after earlier landmark loss at trial over addictive claims

A Florida teen whose lawsuit claimed Meta’s platforms were to blame ⁠for his depression ⁠and anxiety ​dropped his case against the company just days before the trial in Los Angeles was ⁠set to start, his attorneys said on Wednesday. It was the latest in a massive series of high-stakes lawsuits against social media companies for allegedly designing addictive products that lead to the harm of children.

The lawsuit, brought by a 15-year-old boy known as ⁠RKC, originally named four defendants, Google’s YouTube, Meta’s Instagram, Snap Inc’s ​Snapchat and ByteDance’s TikTok. YouTube and TikTok ‌settled in June and Snap reached a tentative settlement in the case, Bloomberg ‌reported on Monday. The terms of those settlements were confidential.

RKC, who started using social media when he was about eight, said he became addicted to it, losing sleep and suffering from depression and anxiety, according ‌to court filings.

“In light of the overall successful result of the litigation and his concerns about ​enduring a grueling weeks-long trial, he has elected to withdraw his claims against Meta,” attorneys for RKC said in a statement. “He’s ready to close this chapter and focus on his recovery ⁠and engage in therapy as he aspires to have a ​normal life.”

A ​spokesperson for Meta said RKC had dropped the claims ​without receiving ‌any payment.

“The claims ​never held ​up,” the company said in a statement. This outcome makes clear that we will not back away from defending ourselves against baseless lawsuits.”

The dropped case comes after Meta and YouTube suffered a bruising loss in March in the same Los Angeles court. That trial lasted six weeks and ended with the two companies being ordered to pay a young woman $6m in damages. In the landmark decision, the jury found Meta and YouTube liable for deliberately designing addictive products and negligent for having failed to provide adequate warnings about the potential dangers of their platforms.

In a separate lawsuit in March brought by New Mexico’s attorney general, a jury ordered Meta to pay $375m in civil penalties over claims that it misled consumers about the safety of its platforms and enabled harm, including child sexual exploitation, against its users. The back-to-back verdicts are the first ever to find social media companies liable for how their products affect young people.

These cases were the first to go to court, and are slated to be followed by more trials from two coordinated groups of more than 2,000 plaintiffs, including families, school districts and state attorneys general, who have brought lawsuits against Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snap.

The four social media companies also settled another major lawsuit just before trial in May, brought by a school district in Kentucky over similar claims of addictive products leading to harm in children.

This month, Meta appealed the verdict in its loss at the Los Angeles court. It challenged the jury’s decision that found the company liable for designing addictive products to hook in young people.

Meta and the other social media companies have vigorously defended their business models, saying their products aren’t addictive. In a post on Wednesday, Andy Stone, Meta’s communications director, wrote that RKC’s claims “never held up” and that he “averaged just minutes a day on Facebook and Instagram”.

Lawyers for RKC said they achieved what they set out to do by bringing awareness to social media’s alleged harms.

“RKC came into this process wanting to hold social media companies accountable and push for changes to protect young people like himself,” the lawyers said. “He did that.”

title: You Can Now Change the Music on Older Instagram Posts
description: You're no longer stuck with that cringe song choice from 2022.
fullText:
For frequent Instagram posters, it might seem like the app has let you add music to posts forever. But in reality, the company only rolled the feature out back in 2022. (If that doesn't sound right to you, you're just misremembering—you have been able to add music to Stories since 2018.) Over the past four years, it has been possible to attach a track to your pictures to set a mood for your post. It's a bit of an Instagram staple at this point: if you use the app with your volume up, you can't really scroll through your friends' posts without hearing a whiplash of songs.

In all that time, however, adding a song was all or nothing. If you posted with a particular tune, that was the permanent soundtrack to your post. Any regrets you might have about that particular song could only be remedied by deleting the post entirely—a bit of an extreme step in most cases. As such, you might have posts in your feed with tracks you don't care for anymore, but since you don't want to take down the pictures altogether, you've had to leave them up and accept your past poor choices. But no more!

On Tuesday, Instagram announced that songs on posts and carousels are now editable. You can swap out songs using Instagram's new "Replace Audio" feature, which lets you change the music on a post without deleting it or affecting any likes or comments. It's a simple change, but one that Instagram's user base will likely receive positively, and positive sentiment is definitely something the company needs in the wake of outcry over another high-profile feature that briefly let users generate AI images with posts from any public account. The company has since removed that option, and seems to be focused on adding new features users might actually want.

Changing the songs on your posts is relatively simple: Any time you want to swap out the song on one of your past posts, you can tap the two lines above the picture, tap "Edit," then choose the new "Original audio" option that appears in the menu. From here, you can change the song to anything in Instagram's library, and, presumably, return here as many times as you like to swap it out again.

On a crowded train of people mostly staring obliviously at our own phones, a stranger had been covertly photographing that little girl over and over again. And if it hadn’t been for that very visible phone screen giving him away, he wouldn’t have been caught.

That encounter was a while ago but my memory was jogged last week listening to a clip of Meta’s VP of wearables, Alex Himel, talk fondly to the BBC about using his new smartglasses to film his daughter singing in a talent contest. They let him capture the memory without having to watch her through a screen, he said, freeing him to be “kind of living in the moment, head up and hands free”. So far, so sweet. But what about the risk of creeps potentially using them to film other people’s daughters covertly, heads up and hands free? Meta’s smartglasses have a tiny flashing warning light on the frame to indicate when the wearer is recording, but the technology is still new enough that many people don’t think to look for it. And in the age of AI, stolen images of children matter. Taken in real life or scraped from the internet, they’re the raw material for generating realistic-looking child abuse material of the most extreme and disturbing kind. (If that sounds like a grim but ultimately fairly victimless crime, the Internet Watch Foundation warned in a recent report that AI-generated material risks fuelling sexual interest in children, normalising violence and increasing the risk of real-life offending.)

When Google launched the first smartglasses in 2013, they didn’t catch on: too nerdy-looking but also potentially too creepy, given the possibilities they afforded stalkers, trolls, criminals gathering intelligence and law enforcement in repressive regimes. But big tech hasn’t given up on the dream of connecting humans more seamlessly to the internet, and newer versions learn from past mistakes. Meta’s are cooler, featuring collaborations with Ray-Ban and Kylie Jenner, and are pitched unashamedly at parents under the wholesome slogan: “never miss a moment”. Want to capture your baby’s milestones, or do all the things you surreptitiously do when you’re with the kids – checking emails, shopping online, listening to podcasts – without taking your eyes off them? It’s an appealing sell to busy, guilty, multi-tasking parents. But the safeguarding concerns around covert filming are real enough for many nurseries and schools to have started banning them from the premises.

A twist in the tale, however, is that making them socially unacceptable risks creating casualties of its own: the technology is potentially life-changing for blind people, helping them navigate confidently around obstacles or instantly translate text to audio.

Meta has argued that it is for individuals to ensure they don’t “actively exploit” the technology, which makes you wonder if it learned anything at all from watching humans get to grips with its social media platforms. Regulatory options might include new privacy legislation designed for the digital age, forcing manufacturers to make it far clearer when the glasses are recording – maybe even with an audible warning, like the beep of a reversing lorry – at least until we’re all primed to look twice at anyone in specs. But since that would make them insufferably embarrassing to wear, it’s unlikely to please tech companies seeking a lucrative mass market.

Another option could be holding manufacturers, not wearers, liable for malicious usage – though that could mean years of painfully slow litigation, concluding long after the damage is done. The nuclear option, meanwhile, would be a before-market regulatory regime for novel technology recognising its capacity for social harm, much as we have for clearing new pharmaceutical drugs or novel foodstuffs.

The best option is arguably the one history suggests is least likely to happen: for a myopic tech industry to start better anticipating, and designing out, potential harms that should be visible from space. There are some things, surely, that nobody needs smartglasses to see.

Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

title: 'Football has lost one of its true greats' - Dalglish pays tribute to Keegan
description: Sir Kenny Dalglish says he is "very saddened" by the passing of former Liverpool forward Kevin Keegan in a personal tribute on Instagram.  "Kevin was one of the very best players of his generation and wore Liverpool's famous number seven shirt with great distinction," Dalglish wrote.
fullText:
Sir Kenny Dalglish says he is "very saddened" by the passing of former Liverpool forward Kevin Keegan in a personal tribute on Instagram.

"Kevin was one of the very best players of his generation and wore Liverpool's famous number seven shirt with great distinction," Dalglish wrote. "His achievements on the pitch were exceptional, but he was also a wonderful person and genuine gentleman.

"Kevin's qualities didn't stop when he finished playing. He went on to become an outstanding manager, and what he built at Newcastle United brought belief, excitement and pride back to the football club.

"He gave so many people wonderful memories and his teams played the game in a way that supporters loved to watch.

"Football has lost one of its true greats."

Keegan's former Liverpool and England team-mate Phil Thompson echoed Dalglish's sentiment and said "it's a difficult time for everybody".

"When I first heard the news, I was absolutely devastated," Thompson said on BBC Radio 5 Live's Football Daily podcast. "But I've been listening to all the tributes and love for Kevin, and about all the love that he gave to everybody else.

"He was a lovely man and that is above all his footballing exploits.

"Humility poured out of Kevin's veins. He was just such a nice guy.

"He never turned down an autograph or photograph. He was the best of all the people I have known in football and in sport.

"There was an honesty in everything about him. He didn't have the greatest ability in the world, but he made the best of what he had which drove him forward. He knew how good he was.

"Even as England manager, he knew his limitations and that is Kevin in a nutshell.

"When he came to Liverpool, he was a star waiting to happen. We got a superhero in 1971 and he was a revelation. He was inspirational.

"He hit it off with Bill Shankly and the two of them were inspired and it took us to new levels. He was the spark the football club needed at the time."

title: This Android App Blocks the Most Addicting Parts of Social Media
description: You can block short-form videos from apps like Instagram and YouTube.
fullText:
I open Instagram to check out my friends' Stories, updates from my local community, and the latest dog video my wife sent me last night. But after doing all of that, I find myself doomscrolling for hours. It got so bad, I ended up deleting the app and using the website exclusively. It's a similar story on YouTube, where I end up scrolling through endless Shorts. When YouTube’s Shorts limit came out, I rushed to enable it.

But I’ve found a better solution for both apps, at least for my Pixel. There’s a setting hidden deep inside the Switchly app that blocks certain addicting elements of popular apps. Switchly is completely free, open-source, and doesn’t show ads: Its main job is to serve as a free and open-source alternative to devices like Brick. It blocks apps and websites to help you focus, and the only way to unblock is by using an NFC tag and a QR code—the Android equivalent of the Foqos iPhone app. Here's how it works.

Switchly can block reels, the Explore page, comments, and Stories on Instagram. On YouTube, it can block Shorts, the Subscriptions page, the "You" tab (YouTube's recommendation feed), and picture-in-picture mode. On X, it can block the home page, search, Grok AI, or notifications. On Snapchat, you can disable the Map, Stories, Spotlight, or the Following page. You can really disable the features that distract you the most. For me, that’s reels, search, and comments on Instagram, and Shorts and the You page on YouTube.

Switchly is an app blocker, so it needs accessibility and screen access permissions before it can work. Because it’s a free and open-source app, with code hosted on GitLab, third-party testers can verify Switchly's security, so I find it safe to use.

Once you grant the app the needed permissions, go to the Blocking tab, then go to the In-app blocking section. Here, enable the features you want to block in each app (this will only work if Switchly’s global blocking is currently disabled). After that, go to the Home page, and from the top, tap Enable. The blocking will now be enabled until you disable it manually.

If, like me, you want to ban these features forever, you can leave it at that. But if you only want to disable them during work hours or on weekdays, you can set up a schedule. If you would like to block certain apps and websites, you can add them from the Manage Apps and Blocked Websites sections. To set up a schedule, go to Manage > Schedules, tap the Plus button, create a new schedule, and customize it to your needs. As we discussed earlier, the app offers many more ruthless options for controlling the block. You can go to Blocking > Blocking Controls to switch to a different blocking method.

fullText:
Midnight to 6am block on some apps is latest stage of Labour’s bid to protect young people from online harms

Sixteen and 17-year-olds are to be encouraged to observe a midnight social media curfew, in the latest stage of Labour’s bid “to protect the next generation” from online harms, including poor sleep caused by night-time scrolling.

From next spring, Britain’s oldest children will be urged to refrain from using certain apps with a midnight to 6am block being switched on by default. But the curfew will not be mandatory and can be overridden. The move is an extension of the under-16 social media ban announced last month, which included restrictions on platforms such as Snapchat, TikTok, YouTube, Instagram, Facebook and X.

The government has also stopped short of restricting the use of virtual private networks, which allow children to avoid social media age gates by pretending they are in a country where there is no ban. The government’s own research found that only 7-10% of children reported using a VPN specifically to bypass age checks. It is also concerned that restrictions could damage free speech.

The Molly Rose Foundation, an internet safety campaign group, said the latest measures were part of “yet another piecemeal set of announcements, not the comprehensive plan for children’s safety that’s required”.

The specific apps covered by the default curfew have not been named in the announcement from the technology secretary, Liz Kendall, in one of the final acts of the Keir Starmer government. Kendall said features that can keep users scrolling for longer – such as videos that automatically play when another one ends and feeds that continually serve up personalised content – will also be switched off by default for older teenagers. However, they will also be able to override that restriction in a couple of clicks. The government is concerned to avoid a “cliff edge” of teenagers suddenly being exposed to social media’s most addictive features the moment they turn 16.

Beeban Kidron, who founded the 5Rights Foundation, which campaigns for child rights online, said having a default that can be switched off was “for show and headlines, not for children”.

“This is not the change that parents asked for, nor experts wanted – it has been cooked up in DSIT [the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology] for another news round.”

Kendall said a public consultation had shown that even as young people gain greater independence at 16, parents and children still want protections from the most addictive online features that can harm their wellbeing.

“These measures will be crucial in helping young people get the sleep they need, focus on school and college, and spend more quality time with family and friends,” she said.

Campaigners are also calling for the government to increase protections for young people against AI chatbots, but Kendall only announced plans for “regular breaks for under-18s using chatbots, encouraging healthier online habits”.

In May, the DSIT commissioned data and market research company Savanta to test three different social media restrictions: rationing to 15 minutes a day, a no-access curfew from 9pm to 7am and complete deletion of social media apps.

Curfews were found to be the most manageable restrictions to enforce, and restricting access to Snapchat, TikTok, Instagram, Facebook, X and Reddit also gave the strongest and most consistent benefit to quality of sleep. YouTube, Teams, Google Classroom and messaging apps, such as WhatsApp and iMessage, were still allowed under the curfew, which in the test ran from 9pm to 7am.

The upsides included young people saying they went to bed earlier, felt more rested, concentrated better in lessons and during revision, and felt less stress. Participants often described these effects as cumulative. Inside households, there was more in-person interaction and shared family time.

Downsides included children feeling isolated and disconnected from friendships when cut off from platforms such as Snapchat, and experiencing irritability and mood fluctuations, with some parents likening the initial adjustment to withdrawal.

fullText:
Lawsuit filed by dozens of employees says people who took maternity or disability leave were disproportionately selected for layoffs

Dozens of Meta employees have sued the social media company over claims that it used artificial intelligence tools to tag workers for mass layoffs. The workers allege that those AI tools targeted them after they asked for protected or maternity leave or disability accommodation.

The lawsuit, filed Monday in federal court in the northern district of California, points to Meta’s workforce reduction of about 8,000 employees earlier this year. Meta is the parent company of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. The suit alleges that Meta used a “constellation of internal artificial intelligence systems”, including AI performance ratings and keystroke- and activity-monitoring data, to pinpoint who to lay off.

“Meta did not assemble the termination list through the considered judgment of managers who knew the work,” reads the 71-page complaint. Instead, the 26 workers listed in the lawsuit allege the company used AI systems “to score, rank and select employees for inclusion on the list”.

The plaintiffs are seeking a preliminary court ruling to stop Meta from finalizing the layoffs while they pursue their ​claims, along with relief that could include reinstatement, back pay, lost equity, benefits and other damages.

AI decision-making in the workplace is becoming an increasingly fraught issue as employees raise concerns about bias, privacy and trust, and regulators are scrutinizing the legality of such tools. States, including California, Colorado and Illinois, have passed laws or regulations within the last couple of years seeking to protect workers from AI-related bias and “automated decision systems”.

The lawsuit against Meta alleges that the company’s AI tools gather data on employees’ performance rankings, productivity and other metrics, and that those inputs do not exist when workers are on medical or family leave. For people with disabilities, those metrics might be reduced.

“The result was that employees who took protected leaves were disproportionately selected for layoff, based on scoring that not only failed to account for their protected leaves, but in effect penalized the employees for exercising their legal rights to these leaves,” reads the complaint.

One of the plaintiffs is a scientist who was on approved pre-birth pregnancy leave – she was notified of her layoff just two days before she gave birth. Another plaintiff is an engineer who said he received a “lowered rating” because of time he took off for an injury. Another, a manager on medical leave, said he was let go 16 days into his time off.

A Meta spokesperson disputed the allegations. “These claims lack merit and are not based on facts,” he said in an email to the Guardian. “Workforce management and organizational decisions were and are made by people, not AI.”

Meta introduced its AI employee-monitoring program earlier this year. It was designed to capture workers’ keystrokes, mouse activity, browser history, along with messages, emails and location data on company devices. Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s CEO, said the idea was to train the company’s AI systems on its employees’ behaviors.

“The AI models learn from watching really smart people do things,” Zuckerberg said in an internal meeting, according to the Information. “The average intelligence of the people who are at this company is significantly higher than the average set of people that you can get to do tasks.”

The lawsuit claims Meta quietly launched the monitoring program without employee buy-in. Meta told employees about it through a “low-visibility internal post – made by an engineer rather than a senior leader”, reads the complaint. “On at least some teams, employees received no consent or acknowledgment prompt at all, and, at least initially, there was no way to opt out.”

Employee backlash quickly racked up over the last few months, prompting Zuckerberg to announce that he was pausing the program in June. His about-face came after more than 1,600 employees signed a petition saying the program violated their privacy.

In Monday’s suit, lawyers for the plaintiffs asked the court to immediately approve an independent audit into Meta’s AI tools. They say it would provide clarification into why the 26 workers, who were on leave or approved for disability accommodation, were let go. “Meta deliberately kept the mechanics of its selection process secret from its employees,” the lawyers said in an emailed statement.

The plaintiffs are still Meta employees until 22 July, when their termination is set to begin, according to the lawyers. Citing retaliation concerns, the attorneys are asking the judge to allow the plaintiffs to remain anonymous and for a court-order to preserve the workers’ employment status while arbitration is pending.

“Once these separations are final, the harms are irreversible: employer-subsidized health coverage lost during pregnancy, postpartum recovery, and active medical treatment; time-bound leave rights extinguished; unvested equity forfeited; and immigration consequences triggered,” the lawyers said.

fullText:
Meta was criticised for feature launched on Tuesday that automatically lets users generate images using content from public Instagram accounts

Meta has said ⁠it is discontinuing an AI feature launched this week that allowed users to generate images using public Instagram ⁠accounts, after drawing widespread ⁠criticism over ​privacy concerns, including from a Hollywood union.

“Our intent was to provide a useful creative tool and to give people control ⁠over whether their public content could be referenced in this way,” Meta said in a statement.

“We’ve heard the feedback that ⁠this feature missed the mark, so it’s no longer available,” it said.

Meta, owner ​of Facebook and Instagram, had launched ‌Muse Image on Tuesday, its ‌first image-generation model from Meta Superintelligence Labs. The feature, integrated into its Meta ‌AI chatbot, can use photos as input and lets users edit generated images directly through sketches.

The feature soon faced backlash over privacy concerns and being an automatic opt-in for users.

Emmy-winning actor Hannah Einbinder, known for Hacks, criticised the feature on Instagram, saying it had been turned on automatically and urging users to ‌turn it off.

SAG-AFTRA, the union representing actors and other media professionals, also urged members and other Instagram users on Thursday to opt ​out of the feature.

“Anything other than a clear and conspicuous opt-in for these types of uses of Instagram users’ images is unacceptable, and an utter miscalculation of public sentiment regarding the obvious dangers and harms inherent in such use,” SAG-AFTRA ⁠said.

Following Meta’s decision to remove the feature, SAG-AFTRA welcomed the move.

“With ​the dangers of nonconsensual ​digital replicas well known to ​all, a feature that encouraged that behavior is unwise. We appreciate ​its discontinuance. It ‌is the responsible ​thing to do,” ​a union spokesperson said.

The reversal reflects increasing pressure on technology companies to give users clear control over how their publicly shared content is used by AI features.

title: Meta pulls new AI image feature after days of backlash
description: Meta's release this week of an AI feature that let people alter Instagram content drew swift blowback.
fullText:
Meta has abruptly taken down a new feature that allowed people to use its artificial intelligence (AI) tool to make fake images from user content on Instagram.

The feature was part of a broad rollout of Muse Image, a new AI image generation tool Meta released on Tuesday as part of Meta AI, the company’s chatbot.

It allowed Meta AI users to tag public-facing accounts on Instagram and quickly use content on those accounts to create AI-generated or altered content and images.

The feature quickly sparked blowback. So much so that Meta has now admitted it “missed the mark, so it’s no longer available”.

“Our intent was to provide a useful creative tool and to give people control over whether their public content could be referenced in this way,” Meta added in its decision to pull the feature. “We've heard the feedback.”

When Meta announced the feature days ago, it said it was limited to Instagram, but more AI features and integrations were planned for WhatsApp, Facebook and Messenger.

It also has an AI video tool in development.

title: Meta found to breach EU laws with 'addictive' Instagram, Facebook designs
description: Instagram and Facebook's "addictive" designs have put Meta in breach of the European Union's digital laws, the EU concluded Friday in a preliminary report.
fullText:
Instagram and Facebook's "addictive" designs have put Meta in breach of the European Union's digital laws, the EU concluded Friday in a preliminary report.

The tech giant violated the EU's Digital Services Act by failing to adequately consider the risks associated with design features that affected the physical well-being of its users, including minors and vulnerable adults, the European Commission said.

These features include infinite scroll, which constantly shows fresh content, autoplay, push notifications and highly personalized recommendation systems — feeding users' compulsion to continue using platforms and putting them into "autopilot mode."

The EU Commission also accused Meta of ignoring available information about how much time young people are spending on Instagram or Facebook at night, and how different types of content formats, from reels to stories, could lead to excessive use of its services.

It adds that Meta hasn't done enough to mitigate these risks and needs to change the design of its features, going as far as disabling "autoplay" and "infinite scroll" by default and enforcing "screen time breaks."

Meta is facing a fine of up to 6% of its total annual turnover if the Commission's findings are confirmed.

"We disagree with these preliminary findings, which don't accurately take into account the significant steps we've taken to protect teens," a spokesperson from Meta said.

Since the investigation began, Meta has rolled out Teen Accounts that "automatically protect teens and put parents in control" by allowing them to block access at night and cap daily screen time at 15 minutes, the tech giant said.

"We share the European Commission's commitment to providing teens with safe, positive online experiences and will continue to engage constructively with them," it added.

This is the second time this year that the EU Commission has found Meta to have breached its rules; in April, it said the company had failed to prevent under-13s from accessing its platforms.

Meta has faced a slew of intense scrutiny over its handling of the safety of users on its platforms this year, including two high-profile U.S. court rulings in March. The first found that the platform's design contributed to addiction and mental health harms in young people, while the other determined that it misled users about children's safety on its platforms.

Meta told CNBC at the time that it disagrees with the findings: "We're clear that Instagram and Facebook are intended for people aged 13 and older and we have measures in place to detect and remove accounts from anyone under that age."

title: Wyoming officials say Meta’s 715,000-square-foot data center is responsible for contaminating its water system with a rare bacterium
description: Cheyenne's Board of Public Utilities tightened its wastewater discharge policy following the discovery of Cupriavidus gilardii in its treatment facility earlier this year.
fullText:
Cheyenne, Wyoming, officials say Meta's data center construction is responsible for the contamination of part of the town's recycled water system.

The Board of Public Utilities (BOPU) traced the presence of a bacterium discovered in its wastewater treatment facility earlier this year to Goat Systems LLC, a Meta contractor for the tech company's in-progress 715,000-square-foot data center campus, according to recent public notices from the BOPU.

The bacterium did not enter Cheyenne's drinking water supply and was found in systems used for irrigation purposes only. Cupriavidus gilardii is a rare organism typically found naturally in water and soil. Infections from this bacterium are extremely rare, BOPU said, but can pose a threat to elders and immunocompromised individuals directly exposed to it.

It was discovered during routine testing in February, prompting BOPU to temporarily suspend the city's reclaimed water irrigation program and terminate Meta's discharge privileges.

The board also announced last week it would not accept industrial wastewater discharges associated with fill-and-flush operations—which circulates, then flushes purified water to eliminate construction debris and residue—nor closed-loop cooling systems popular in data centers that circulate coolants mixed with water.

The board classified the incident as "significant non-compliance with federal pretreatment regulations."

"Over the past two months, BOPU staff have undertaken significant remediation efforts, including draining and disinfecting the entire reuse water system and Prairie View Pond to eliminate any remaining bacterial presence," one notice said.

Cheyenne's BOPU declined Fortune's request for comment and said it will hold a press conference in the next week with additional details on the situation.

A Meta spokesperson told Fortune the company is supporting Fortis, its general contractor, in its efforts to resolve the problem, and that Fortis began testing its own water through a third-party environmental specialist, who found no traces of the bacterium.

"When the board shared that it found a substance in the city's wastewater—not public drinking water—Fortis immediately stopped discharging industrial wastewater and began hauling it offsite," a spokesperson said in a statement. "Meta is committed to being a good neighbor in Cheyenne, including through the protection of local water resources, and will continue encouraging collaboration between Fortis and the board until this situation is resolved."
